summary: This document describes information security services for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP), which offers RESTful web services for registration data from domain name and regional internet registries. It covers access control, authentication, and related matters.

eli5.summary: Registration lookups may include sensitive details. This describes how to check who is asking and how to protect the answers.

subtitle: How RDAP gets access control, authentication, confidentiality and integrity by leaning on HTTP and TLS.

tldr.problem: WHOIS has no features for controlling access, identifying clients, or protecting data in transit, and it has historically exposed registrants' personal data to the public.
tldr.mechanism: RDAP has no native security services. It relies on other layers: HTTP authentication (Basic or Digest), optional TLS client certificates, and HTTP over TLS for confidentiality and integrity.
tldr.outcome: Operators can offer tiered access, protect traffic and mark redacted data, but policy is up to each operator. The RFC is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Client auth schemes
facts.value: Must support both Basic and Digest

today: RFC 7481 is an Internet Standard and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the security companion to RFC 7480.

sections.title: Security Goals and Approach
sections.content:
RFC 7481 is part of the RDAP document set along with RFC 7480, RFC 7482 and RFC 7483. One goal of RDAP is to provide security services that WHOIS lacks: access control, authentication, authorization, availability, data confidentiality and data integrity.

The central point of Section 3 is that RDAP itself does not include native security services. It relies on features available in other protocol layers, and additional or alternative mechanisms can be added in the future. No requirements were identified for other security services.
sections.eli5: RDAP does not build its own lock. It uses the strong locks that already come with the web.

sections.title: Access Control and Authentication
sections.content:
WHOIS has no features to identify clients or control access. RDAP lets server operators identify, authenticate and authorize clients and then control access. Returned information can be marked with a status value showing the access granted. The RFC does not dictate operator policy: an operator with no tiered-access policy needs no authentication.

RDAP clients and servers MUST implement the HTTP authentication framework of RFC 7235. The basic scheme sends a user name and password in base64-encoded form, and the digest scheme authenticates without exposing the plaintext password. Servers MUST support either Basic or Digest, not necessarily both; clients MUST support both. If Basic is used, HTTP over TLS MUST be used to protect the credentials.

TLS client certificates (X.509) are an optional way to authenticate clients. For server authentication, RDAP adds no unique requirements: transports must provide TLS (such as HTTPS) or an equivalent level of server authentication.
sections.eli5: A service can ask visitors to show a password or a special card. The password must only be shown through a sealed envelope, which is what TLS provides.

sections.title: Federated Authentication
sections.content:
With ordinary authentication a client needs separate credentials for every RDAP server, which becomes unwieldy as servers multiply. RDAP MAY include a federated mechanism so one credential works across servers in the same federation. Any such mechanism MUST be fully supported by HTTP.

The RFC names OAuth (RFC 6749), OpenID, SAML 2.0 and certificate-authority-based approaches as possible. At the time of publication, negotiation or advertisement of federated authentication services was still undefined by those protocols, and developing it is beyond the scope of the document. OAuth and OpenID do not consistently require confidentiality, so HTTP over TLS can be used against man-in-the-middle attacks.

With certificates, multiple RDAP servers can trust the same certificate authorities, so any client holding a certificate from a trusted CA can access any server in the federation.
sections.eli5: It is like one library card that works at every library in town, instead of a separate card for each.

sections.title: Authorization and Availability
sections.content:
Server operators MAY offer varying degrees of access depending on policy and need. If they do, the server MUST provide granular access controls, meaning per registration data object. The examples given: clients see only data they have a relationship with; anonymous access may yield no contact information; full access may go to a special group of authenticated clients.

For availability, RDAP adds no unique requirements, but operators should be aware of denial of service and read RFC 4732. A service MAY throttle a single client's queries. If it does, it SHOULD return HTTP 429, and a client that receives 429 SHOULD slow down and honor Retry-After. This is not a defense against a malicious client that ignores it, and a server may use a different code to avoid revealing that rate limiting is the reason.
sections.eli5: Different visitors can be allowed to see different amounts, record by record. If someone asks too fast, the server can tell them to slow down.

sections.title: Confidentiality and Integrity
sections.content:
WHOIS cannot protect data from disclosure or modification in transit. RDAP uses HTTP over TLS (RFC 2818) for both. HTTP over TLS MUST be used to protect all client-server exchanges unless operational constraints make that impossible. It must also be used when the operator's policy requires encryption or message integrity.

Integrity has one especially specific need: assurance that HTTP 30x redirection hints and response elements are not modified in transit.

Object-level protection is possible, such as encrypting or signing discrete objects like path segments and JSON responses, but there are no current requirements for object-level confidentiality or integrity. Support could be added in the future.
sections.eli5: TLS is a sealed, tamper-evident envelope around everything sent. The RFC says to use it nearly always.

sections.title: Privacy Threats
sections.content:
Registration data has historically included personal data about registrants, and WHOIS has made it public without authentication or access control. As a result, proxy and privacy services arose to shield registrants' identities.

RDAP does not change what data operators may require registrants to supply, but it supports mechanisms that can reduce privacy risk if operators choose to use them. Clients can be authenticated, so not all data need be public. Status values can show that returned data is private (not for public consumption), redacted (some fields withheld), obscured (altered so as not to readily reveal the real data) or registered by a proxy.

Operators may also collect fewer fields or leave fields unpopulated, since many jCard fields may be irrelevant. People who query are at risk too: a registry employee's query may reveal activity they would prefer to keep private, which HTTP over TLS helps protect.
sections.eli5: Old lookups showed everyone's home details to anyone. RDAP lets a service hide, blur or limit those details and tell you when it has.

sections.title: Remaining Risks
sections.content:
Non-repudiation was considered and rejected for lack of requirements, although some deployed WHOIS servers can return signed responses with proof of origin, and RDAP might be extended to provide this in the future.

As an HTTP-based protocol, RDAP is susceptible to code injection attacks such as SQL, shell and HTML-script injection. Confidentiality and integrity help against man-in-the-middle injection, but software vulnerabilities on either side can still allow injection. Consistently checking server credentials helps detect man-in-the-middle attacks.

Certificate-based federation has a risk: too promiscuous or even rogue CAs may be included in the list a TLS server sends to clients. Periodic monitoring of the trusted-CA list helps.
sections.eli5: Even with good locks, bad programs can still be tricked, and a lock-maker you trust too much might be a fake. So check carefully and review who you trust.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: HTTP Basic or Digest; optional TLS client certificates.

items.title: Authorization
items.text: Per-object access controls chosen by the operator.

items.title: Availability
items.text: Optional throttling with HTTP 429 and Retry-After.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: HTTP over TLS for client-server exchanges.

items.title: Integrity
items.text: HTTP over TLS protects redirects and responses.
